newsitem.title: GERMANY: Hochtief beats profit forecast on growth abroad.
newsitem.headline: Hochtief beats profit forecast on growth abroad.

text.p: German construction group Hochtief AG said on Tuesday that its 1996 net profit beat expectations, rising 6.8 percent to 146.1 million marks ($84.6 million) as a result of strong international growth.

The company, which had expected unchanged profits, also said orders in the first quarter of 1997 climbed 37.6 percent to 3.2 billion marks, while output in the period increased 7.8 percent to 2.6 billion marks.

But the outlook for 1997 was cautious because of the weak domestic economy, industry-wide structural change and intense price competition in Germany, chief executive Hans-Peter Keitel said at a news conference.

"The result this year should at least hold to the 1996 level," he said. "The difficult situation in the German construction industry will not improve in 1997. We will face great problems. We must accept the fact that we are in a structural crisis."

Hochtief's overseas orders rose 37.1 percent last year to 7.10 billion marks, while overseas output increased 25.3 percent to 4.96 billion marks. International units contributed half of the 1996 orders total of 14.32 billion marks, and 40 percent of the 12.18 billion marks in total output.
In contrast, German orders rose 9.9 percent to 7.22 billion marks and output was up only 1.6 percent to 7.22 billion marks.
Keitel said he expected German orders to remain at least level in 1997.
Pierre Drach, an analyst at Independent Research in Frankfurt, said he expected a moderate improvement in results in 1997, despite weakness in Germany.
"I was surprised by the international orders for 1996," he told Reuters. "The potential is there for growth for the full year, even if the first quarter increase was not exhorbitant."
Hochtief was counting on its proposed partnership with German rival Phillip Holzmann AG to keep overseas growth on the rise, Keitel said.
"Cooperation offers strengths in foreign markets," he said. "We can increase our synergies relatively quickly in various markets like China and Latin America."

Hochtief planned to pool its 24.9 percent stake of Holzmann shares with a 25.1 percent stake owned by Deutsche Bank AG. The company sought to form an international partnership, although the firms would remain separate and compete in Germany.
The deal is subject to approval by the European Union and could face opposition from Germany's cartel office.
Drach said he expected the cartel office to intervene strongly against the deal. "They see it as a German matter."

To improve its domestic situation, Hochtief said it was planning to expand a restructuring. It would form new construction materials and equipment service units this year, after forming separate project development, software and highway construction companies in 1996, Drach said.
He said the firm had reduced its network of subsidiaries and pooled its know-how into distinct centres.
But Hochtief said that consolidation in German construction had caused prices to fall one percent even though costs have risen.
The firm's worldwide payroll rose 1.1 percent to 40,785 last year, although it cut its domestic workforce by 10.5 percent, or 2,300 jobs.

The job reductions cost 130 million marks in restructuring charges that were offset by the sale of subsidiaries such as its Dames & Moore engineering unit in the United States. The company also wrote off 323 million marks related to its shareholdings in Holzmann and other units, improving its financial reserves.
